cards.title: Suicide rates highest ever among middle-aged men

The figures for England and Wales showed **6,162 suicide deaths** registered in 2025, down from 6,190 last year; the overall rate remained broadly the same at 11.3 per 100,000. cards.title: Anthropic's Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke

The author says Scion’s **“derived data”** resembles Mononoke, which they helped build at Meta; they say Anthropic credited Sapling but **left Mononoke unmentioned**. cards.title: Why is every rationalist blog post way too long?

depth.text: someone argues rationalist bloggers **write too much** instead of questioning their **starting assumptions**

Alex Wennerberg says he cut around **70%** of his draft; his piece was 2,700 words, after he skimmed Scott Alexander’s **25,000-word post**. He argues **verbosity** can stand in for thoroughness, while the community prizes unconventional ideas over common sense and tradition.

cards.camps: Two camps: critics say rationalist writing is bloated and tedious; defenders say detail and nuance matter, and argue the author dismisses careful arguments too easily.

comments.text: > adding layers of detail and nuance rather than interrogating the one or two assumptions they make at the start or broadening their philosophical background beyond the collection of texts popular within their subculture. Personally i think the world would be a better place if more of us added nuance to our arguments.

> Eliezer Yudkowsky's "sequences" are over one million words long. This is a particularly weird example. The median post in the "sequences" is less than 1000 words long. The sequences are mostly a long series of individually very short blogposts.

The Economist is so good in this respect. A smart, very good writer will write something and get to the point quickly. Articles are mostly a page or less. Writing like that respects people's time. Many bloggers could do with writing things more briefly. The author of this piece also makes a very good point that often long pieces go into weird corners of their own argument without thinking about…

"The idea that something may be true, valuable, or good merely because it is common sense or inherited tradition is anathema to them" This is reasonable though. Tradition and common sense suggest value perhaps more than rationalists think, but if tradition and common sense have value, there is an underlying reason.

Agree with the author. Most rationalist material I've tried to read it's incredibly lengthy and frequently boring. It's also true that they are using verbosity and a certain academic style to hide the lack of precision and correctness. They are prolific writers, but not great.

cards.title: Why do LLM pelicans look like this?

depth.text: someone says **AI pelicans** keep coming out **alike**, even when a simple prompt leaves room for variety

The post compares SVGs from the same pelican-and-bicycle prompt and calls the similar results **“diversity collapse.”** Its UI-design benchmark puts the best model at **65.5**, against **92.3** for a human reference.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say a plain prompt should get a plain pelican and variation should be requested; others say the repeated compositions point to a real lack of model diversity.

comments.text: I'm not clear on what the claim is here. The article faults LLMs for not being more creative (riding in the city in the rain, in East Asia, in outer space, etc.). But, if prompted, "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle," with no additional details or specification, then I would _expect_ something generic: a side view, nondescript terrain or perhaps terrain associated with a pelican…

The lack of variety is probably the most underrated issue, and the most likely cause of annoying patterns you all hate. All current post-trained LLMs are mode-collapsed compared to the post-training set distribution, and this doesn't get nearly enough attention from the labs and independent researchers. It's far from being a transformer-only problem, it's a common failure mode in all kinds of…

The example just doesn't support the claim. If I ask for a pelican riding a bicycle, I am expecting a relatively boring image of a pelican riding a bicycle, not a pelican flying through a thunderstorm while on a bicycle. That's just straight up not what I asked for. I didn't ask it to be creative, when I imagine myself riding a bicycle, I'm not flying! If I added "be creative and unique, you can…

It is fairly easy to go ask for a differently styled pelican, environment, background, etc. But that's not the point. I was thinking just today about how, if I could hire my competition's lead designer/programmers, have them design a system for me cleanroom, that I'd effectively know everything there is to know about my competition's limitations. This is trivial to do with LLMs. "Make me a thing…
A good prompt will shift the distribution away from average eg: https://john.hartnup.uk/2026/06/07/ai-event-posters.html This is a feature, not a bug.

glossary.on-device: Runs on the phone or computer itself, rather than sending the work elsewhere.
glossary.active parameters: The portion of an AI model it uses to produce each piece of an answer.
glossary.MoE: Mixture of Experts: a model with many specialist parts that sends each piece of text to only a few of them.
glossary.agentic: Describes AI that chooses steps and acts toward a task, rather than only answering a question.
glossary.tokens/s: Tokens per second: a rough measure of how quickly a model produces text.
glossary.benchmark: A test people use to compare how well different tools do a task.
glossary.reward hacking: When an AI finds a way to get a high score without doing what its designers actually wanted.
glossary.sandbox: A separate, contained space where software can be tested without affecting the rest of a computer or system.
glossary.quantization: A way to make a model use less computing power by representing its internal numbers less precisely.
glossary.pair programming: Two people work on the same code together, sharing ideas or control.
glossary.self-host: Run a service on computers you manage yourself.
glossary.fork: A separate copy of a shared software project that people can take in a different direction.
glossary.LiveKit: A service Petal can use to send media between people in a shared session.
glossary.IME: Input Method Editor: a tool that lets someone type using a popup to choose characters or words.
glossary.CJK: Chinese, Japanese, and Korean, grouped together here because their writing systems need special search support.
glossary.grapnel: A hooked tool dragged along the seabed to catch a cable so a ship can lift it.
glossary.territorial waters: The sea area a country controls near its coast, where cable work needs its permission.
glossary.choke point: A narrow route that many cables pass through, so damage there can affect several at once.
glossary.ISO: A disk-image file that can hold a copy of a disc’s contents.
glossary.kernel exploit: A way to use a flaw in the core of an operating system to make it do something it should not.
glossary.checksum offload: A feature that lets network hardware calculate checksums instead of the computer’s main processor.
glossary.TCP checksum: Transmission Control Protocol checksum: a small value used to check whether data sent over a network was damaged.
glossary.TLS: Transport Layer Security: a way to scramble information as it travels between devices, so others can’t read it.
glossary.MAC: Message Authentication Code: a short check attached to data that can help show whether it was changed.
glossary.ECC RAM: Error-Correcting Code RAM: memory that can detect and fix some errors in stored data.
glossary.NIC: Network Interface Card: the part of a computer that connects it to a network.
glossary.cache coherency: Keeping copies of data used by different parts of a computer in agreement.
glossary.DMA: Direct Memory Access: a way for a device to move data into or out of memory without the main processor handling every step.
glossary.OpenWRT: Software for managing routers, often used instead of the software supplied by the maker.
glossary.SSH: Secure Shell: a way to connect to another computer and send it commands over a network.
glossary.firmware: The built-in software that tells a device's hardware how to work.
glossary.driver: Software that lets a computer communicate with a piece of hardware.
glossary.TUI: Terminal User Interface: the menus and controls an app shows inside a text terminal.
glossary.client/server model: A setup where one background program does the work for several apps that connect to it.
glossary.code mode: A way for the agent to write one script that calls tools and handles their results together.
glossary.plugin: An add-on that gives an app extra tools or features.
glossary.subagent: A helper assigned a smaller part of a larger task.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI apps to connect to outside tools.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.anomie: A feeling of unease when familiar social rules stop giving people a clear guide for how to live.
glossary.suicidal ideation: Thoughts about suicide, whether or not someone has made a plan.
glossary.per 100,000: A way to compare rates between groups of different sizes by expressing the count as if each group had 100,000 people.
glossary.source control: Tools for keeping track of changes to code and helping developers work on it together.
glossary.derived data: Information worked out from other stored information, so a system can reuse it instead of doing the work again.
glossary.monorepo: One repository that holds code for many projects or services.
glossary.prior art: Earlier work or ideas that are relevant to a new design.
glossary.sampling frame: The list or pool a survey starts from when choosing whom to ask.
glossary.post-stratification weighting: A way of adjusting survey answers afterward so the group better matches the people the survey is meant to represent.
glossary.parasocial relationship: A one-sided feeling of closeness with someone who does not know you personally.
glossary.rationalist: In this discussion, someone who puts a lot of weight on reasoning and questioning assumptions.
glossary.heterodox: An idea that goes against what most people in a community usually believe.
glossary.prolixity: A way of writing that uses more words than needed.
glossary.UX: User experience: how using a product feels and how easy it is to get things done.
glossary.office suite: A set of programs for tasks like writing, spreadsheets and presentations.
glossary.llms.txt: A text file a website can offer for AI tools to read to learn about the site.
glossary.URL: A web address; here, the address can also carry a document.
glossary.PDF annotation: A note or mark added to a PDF file.
glossary.ASN: Autonomous System Number: a number used to identify a network on the internet.
glossary.JA4 fingerprint: A recognizable pattern in how software connects securely to a website, which can help spot the same software using another network.
glossary.WAF: Web Application Firewall: a website’s guard that checks incoming requests and can block suspicious ones.
glossary.bot traffic: Web requests made automatically by software rather than by a person.
glossary.API header: Application Programming Interface header: a setting sent along with a request that helps a service understand what to do with it.
glossary.flag: A switch that turns a feature on or off.
glossary.bounding box: A rectangle that marks where an element should appear in an image.
glossary.context length: How much text a model can take into account at once.
glossary.production: The live version of software that people are actually using.
glossary.rare earths: A group of metals used in specialized materials; separating them from ore takes a lot of processing.
glossary.CoCo bond: A loan that can turn into part ownership of a company if agreed conditions are met.
glossary.offtake agreement: A deal where a buyer promises to purchase a producer’s output.
glossary.price floor: A guaranteed minimum price for what a producer sells.
glossary.chokepoint: A part of a supply chain where one party can block or slow goods and hurt others who rely on them.
glossary.pro rata: A share divided in proportion to how much each participant is entitled to.
glossary.StarShield: The military package for satellite terminals discussed in the article.
glossary.UAV: Unmanned aerial vehicle: a drone that flies without a person aboard.
glossary.GNSS: Global Navigation Satellite System: satellite signals that help a device work out where it is.
glossary.inertial systems: Equipment that estimates movement and direction using changes it senses inside the device.
glossary.data link: The connection that lets an operator send instructions to a drone and receive information back.
glossary.geofencing: Setting virtual boundaries that a device or service can enforce based on where it is.
glossary.mesh radio: A radio setup where devices pass messages between one another, letting information travel across several devices.
glossary.BOM: Bill of Materials: a list of the parts needed to build something.
glossary.LEO: Low Earth orbit: a region fairly close to Earth where satellites travel around the planet.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.SVG: Scalable Vector Graphics: a picture format that stays sharp when resized.
glossary.UI: User interface: the screens and controls people use to operate a device.
glossary.mode collapse: When a model keeps producing similar results instead of showing much variety.
glossary.RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: a way to train an AI by having people rate its answers.
glossary.post-training: Extra training after a model's initial training that shapes how it responds.
glossary.frontier model: One of the most capable, newest AI models available.
